title: PHP2Shell: the PHP updates WordPress sites need now
excerpt: PHP2Shell affects PHP beneath WordPress. Find the fixed releases, a hosting checklist and a request for proof that your live site has both patches.
metaDescription: PHP2Shell affects the PHP runtime behind WordPress. Check fixed versions, get a request to send your host, and confirm that your live site runs the patch.

blocks.text: **PHP2Shell requires an urgent PHP update if your website runs an affected version.** The first fixed releases are **8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12**, published on October 21, 2026. For WordPress owners, the immediate action is to have the host confirm that the PHP runtime serving the site includes both fixes. [PHP release notice](https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php).

A fully updated WordPress dashboard leaves that question open. PHP runs beneath WordPress, and your host or server administrator controls its installation. This guide explains the two flaws, the evidence to request, and what webvise found when checking its own website.

**Reviewed October 22, 2026.** This article covers [CVE-2026-109618](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-109618) and [CVE-2026-109619](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-109619), known as PHP2Shell. The technical details below follow the PHP project's advisories.

items: Update the PHP runtime and verify what the live website runs. A WordPress or plugin update alone cannot establish that these fixes are installed.
Both CVEs concern PHP memory handling. Their triggers and the demonstrated attack paths differ.
A hosting vendor may backport the fixes to a package with an older PHP version number. Ask for its security advisory and package revision.
Patch the existing site first. Consider a migration separately, once the immediate exposure has been addressed.

blocks.text: Which PHP versions fix PHP2Shell?

The PHP project released fixes for four supported branches. Match your installed branch to its first fixed release in the [official announcement](https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php). Later releases on that branch can also include the fixes.

Distribution packages need a second check. A vendor can apply the security fixes while retaining an older upstream version number, so obtain the package revision and an advisory naming both CVEs. A number alone can give the wrong answer in either direction.

PHP 8.1 and older have reached upstream end of life. For this incident, the PHP team provided limited source backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1. Ask your vendor about packaged fixes and plan a move to a supported branch; those exceptional patches do not restore ongoing upstream support.
What is the difference between the two CVEs?

**CVE-2026-109618 concerns interrupted memory initialization.** An out-of-memory failure can leave PHP's internal request data only partly initialized. Cleanup can then use that invalid data. The [PHP advisory](https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w) reports unauthenticated remote code execution against Apache mod_php, including a path that runs before application code starts.

**CVE-2026-109619 concerns state surviving between requests.** A PHP worker can retain references to memory that a previous request has freed. A later request reaching the same worker may use that stale state. The [separate advisory](https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp) reports remote code execution through session lifecycle paths against both mod_php and PHP-FPM.

That distinction matters when a host says it uses FPM. For CVE-2026-109618, the advisory describes FPM as susceptible based on source analysis, without a demonstrated complete FPM exploit. CVE-2026-109619 has a validated FPM path that depends on a suitable application operation. FPM users should apply both fixes.

Both advisories rate the flaws critical at **CVSS v4.0 9.2**. Successful code execution uses the web worker's permissions. Its access to files, secrets and other services determines the damage possible on a particular system.
How should a WordPress owner check the site?

Start in **Tools > Site Health > Info > Server** and record the PHP version. WordPress documents that screen in its [Site Health guide](https://wordpress.org/documentation/article/site-health-screen/). Use the value to open a hosting support request, including the domain and the two CVE IDs.

PHP upgrades happen through the hosting environment. [WordPress's PHP guidance](https://wordpress.org/documentation/update-php/) assigns that step to the host or its control panel. Ask whoever maintains the server to confirm the package actually serving web requests, including any vendor backport.

Check each installation separately. A production shop, staging site and old campaign subdomain can use different PHP pools or hosting accounts. Write down the owner for each one, then keep the provider's confirmation beside the domain it covers.

The PHP project says an update is the complete fix. Its [technical advisories](https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp) describe partial measures for specific paths, with explicit limits. Have the server administrator assess those if an update is delayed; a temporary setting change should never close the patch request.
What webvise checked on its own website

On October 22, webvise checked its landing site's repository and production function runtime. The site uses **Next.js 16 and React**. The inspected Vercel functions reported **nodejs24.x**. The source review followed the blog loader, API handler and database adapter to see which runtime those components actually use.

rows: JSON files loaded through Node's filesystem API
This content path uses Node, with no PHP CMS
tRPC request handler in the Next.js application
No PHP source or Composer manifests found
No PHP application found in this repository

blocks.text: Those findings support a narrow conclusion: **the inspected components do not run PHP**. They establish no security conclusion about unrelated services, other websites or the rest of the infrastructure. Next.js, Node and application dependencies still need their own updates and security review.

The review also checked the technology detection behind webvise's WordPress Health Report. It looks for public clues such as WordPress paths in HTML and PHP-related response headers. It cannot inspect the installed server package or verify a backported fix. Treat a public website scan as a starting point for questions; get patch evidence from the host.
Send your host a request they can answer

A useful reply identifies the running package and confirms deployment. The same principle guided the webvise review: follow the component that serves the request, then state exactly what the evidence covers. Copy and adapt this request for each hosting account.

Please confirm whether the PHP runtime serving [domain] includes the fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Provide the active PHP version and package revision, plus the vendor advisory if you use backported patches. Confirm deployment to every serving instance, including staging and subdomains, with PHP workers restarted or replaced as required. If any installation remains unpatched, identify it and give the expected completion time.

items: Before the change, confirm that a recent backup exists and that someone owns recovery if compatibility problems appear.
After the change, request evidence from the live web runtime. A command-line PHP installation can differ from the one serving the website.
Check the business flows that matter: submitting an inquiry, logging in, uploading media, or completing checkout where applicable.
Keep the package revision, covered domains and completion time in the maintenance record. Escalate an incomplete reply while any installation remains unresolved.

blocks.text: Make that ownership part of the maintenance agreement. webvise's [web application security requirements checklist](/blog/web-application-security-requirements-checklist) explains how to ask for an owner, a check and evidence before handing a system over.
Should this incident prompt a WordPress migration?

Patch first. A well-maintained WordPress site with a host that responds clearly may still suit the business. An urgent PHP advisory alone gives too little information to justify replacing a working website.

For a brochure or lead-generation site, recurring uncertainty about hosting and unused plugins can justify a separate review of the setup. webvise's own blog publishes JSON content through Node. Your team may need different editing tools, integrations or commerce functions.

[webvise's WordPress migration service](/services/wordpress-migration) covers a Next.js rebuild with URL mapping, redirects, metadata, forms and an agreed editing workflow. Removing PHP from a particular application removes that application's dependence on PHP patches. Keeping WordPress as a headless backend retains a PHP system that still needs maintenance.

Once your host has confirmed the fixes, [contact webvise](/#contact) if you want to assess whether a simpler website setup fits your business. Bring the current URL, the features your team uses and the hosting reply.
